title: AMP’s latest buyback signals CFS is now off the table
full_text:
AMP’s half-year result has done more to close down speculation than open it up. The board’s decision to layer a further $150m on-market buyback on top of the one struck earlier in the year, alongside a maiden interim dividend of 3c per share, is being read in deal circles as close to confirmation that an acquisition of Colonial First State is not seriously on the cards.
The subject wasn’t raised once during the analyst Q&A, an absence some see as telling in itself. For a group generating $236m in cash for the half and returning $201m of it to shareholders through dividends and buybacks, the message to the market was one of capital discipline over ambition.
It’s consistent with chief executive Blair Vernon’s comments at the Macquarie conference in May, where he struck a cautious tone on mergers and acquisitions and signalled a preference for organic growth over deal-making.
The bank, however, is a different story, and one still without an ending. Underlying profit at the bank fell to $20m from $30m in the prior corresponding period, continuing to weigh on group earnings.
AMP has never hidden its desire to exit the business, but the stumbling block hasn’t shifted, which is that the group wants a price above book value, and buyers remain unwilling to pay up for a $23bn mortgage book competing against the major banks on scale and funding costs.
There was some detail on how AMP is managing the capital intensity of that business in the interim, with the platforms division shifting toward more securitised funding, including a $79m capital securitisation deal in the half, specifically to hold less regulatory capital, even at some cost to return on equity. It’s a sign AMP is managing the balance sheet more actively rather than working toward a near-term sale.
Put together, the half-year update leaves the state of play largely unchanged. CFS looks further from the agenda than it did before Thursday, and the bank remains for sale in principle, but stuck exactly where it was on price. Shares closed up almost 6 per cent at $2.31.
